# The problem

## Methodological research asserts more than it demonstrates

A methodological paper claims that a procedure works, on the evidence of simulation
studies and/or benchmarks --- that is, \highlight{a computation}.

\vspace{0.4em}
However, the reader receives a PDF with plots/tables, \highlight{not the path that produced them}.

- code and data, when shared at all, are rarely runnable as published
- peer review examines the argument, essentially never the computation
- a year later, the environment has moved and nothing builds

\vspace{0.4em}
::: {.callout-important title="The premise of Computo"}
If the computation is the evidence, then it should also be reviewed --- and it should still run in ten years.
:::

## Computo in one slide

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}

- Created in **2021** under the auspices of the **French Statistical Society** (SFdS)
- **Diamond open access**: free to read, free to publish --- ISSN 2824-7795
- **CC-BY 4.0**, authors retain copyright; DOIs registered with DataCite
- Scope: computational and algorithmic contributions in **statistics and machine learning**
- Open peer review on **OpenReview**; partner of **PCI Statistics and ML**
- \highlight{23 papers published} since April 2022

:::

## What we publish

- **Methods papers** --- original stats/ML developments, or numerical studies that
  illustrate theoretical results
- **Case studies and surveys** --- including \highlight{neutral comparison studies}: when,
  how and why compared methods perform well or less well
- **Software and tutorial papers** --- an implementation *plus* a concrete use case,
  with benchmarking against related work


\vspace{0.5em}
::: {.callout-note title="Primary condition"}
Numerical reproducibility is a \highlight{necessary condition for publication} (neither a badge nor a supplementary file).
:::

# How it works

## The stack

Every submission is a **git repository** that builds itself.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}

1. **Literate programming** --- Quarto: text, equations, code and figures in one source
2. **Pinned environment** --- `renv.lock`, `requirements.txt`, `Project.toml`
3. **Continuous integration** --- rebuilt from scratch on our infrastructure, at every push
4. **Data** --- shipped or deposited (e.g. Zenodo)

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{img/workflow.png}

:::
::::

\vspace{0.3em}
Templates for **R**, **Python** and **Julia**; the workflow itself is language-agnostic.

## Two review tracks, running in parallel

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

\lead{Scientific review}

- Reports are public on OpenReview after acceptance
- Reviewers may stay anonymous
- Papers recommended by *PCI Statistics and ML* are accepted without re-review

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

\lead{Reproducibility check}

- Automated and continuous, from the first submission
- Run by the editorial/tech team, not the referees
- A paper that does not build is not reviewable

:::
::::

\bigskip

::: {.callout-note title="External recognition"}
A 2026 comparative review of reproducibility policies [@hornung2026] ranks Computo among
the \highlight{five journals out of nine} that perform an *independent check* (active, execution-based review) of
results, alongside JSS, JASA, Meta-Psychology and the Biometrical Journal.
:::

## After acceptance: keep reproducibility

- Article repository transferred to `github.com/computorg/`
- DOI registered on DataCite; metadata should make it indexable
- Review reports published alongside the paper
- Repository archived on **Software Heritage**
- Workflows of published articles are \highlight{re-run periodically} to detect decay

\vspace{1em}
::: {.callout-tip title="Long-term reproducibility is a maintenance activity"}
Publishing a reproducible artifact is a one-off event. Keeping the article reproducible requires considerably more effort.
:::

\vspace{0.3em}
We have shown the feasibility of our policy: submissions do build, and keep building.

## What it costs, and what transfers to other fields

The cost falls on the *first* submission: templates absorb most of the technical
burden, and editors gain a new form of check.

\bigskip

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

\lead{Still hard}

- \highlight{Finding authors and reviewers}
- Getting indexed by academic databases
- Heavy computation and large data
- Managing outdated dependencies

:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

\lead{What transfers}

- Nothing in the stack is specific to statistics: only git, notebook templates, a lockfile and CI
- The editorial move that makes the build a condition is the hard part, but it is "free"
- Separating *scientific* review from the *reproducibility* check keeps referee load unchanged
- Diamond needs light infrastructure, a learned-society host and free software

:::
::::
